en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 3.1 (SN 3.1, SN 112, PTS [1st ed. SN i 68, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 157) 1. First Chapter: The Short Discourses (Paṭhamavagga) The Short Discourse (Daharasutta)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
"Does Master Gotama also claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?
"Great King, if one were speaking rightly of anyone who has awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, it is of me that one would rightly say so."
“For I, Great King, have fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. “Master Gotama,
there are those ascetics and brahmins who lead a community, who head a group, who are teachers of a group, who are well-known and famous, founders of sects, esteemed as holy men by the multitude—
namely, Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Pakudha Kaccāyana, and Ajita Kesakambala.”

When they were asked by me, "Do you claim to have fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?", being thus questioned, they did not claim to have fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Why then does Master Gotama, though young in birth and new in his going forth, [claim this]?
"Great King, there are four kinds of people who should not be despised as 'young' nor treated with contempt as 'young':"
Which four?
A khattiya, O Great King, though he be young, is not to be despised; though he be young, he is not to be held in contempt.
A snake, O Great King, though it be young, is not to be despised; though it be young, it is not to be held in contempt.
“Fire, great king, should not be despised because it is young, nor should it be treated with contempt because it is young.
A bhikkhu, great king, should not be despised because he is young, nor should he be treated with contempt because he is young.
These four, great king, should not be despised because they are young, nor should they be treated with contempt because they are young.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
“A kshatriya endowed with noble birth...”
One who is well-born and renowned—
a person should not despise him because he is young, nor should they treat him with contempt.
For it is possible that this lord of men,
a kshatriya who has obtained the kingdom,
being angry, [might punish] with royal punishment.
He becomes exceedingly agitated when that person departs;
therefore, one should avoid such a person,
guarding one's own life.
Whether in a village or in a forest,
wherever one sees a snake,
one should not despise it, thinking, "It is young."
A person should not despise him;
like a serpent of blazing power,
he moves about in various forms.
Thus, having once attacked and bitten a fool—
whether a man or a woman—
one should therefore avoid him.
Protecting his own life from the many-eating,
ensnaring fire with its blackened tracks.
A person should not despise him as being "small," nor should they treat him with contempt;
for he has already acquired the fuel [for rebirth].
Having become a great fire,
it assails and burns the fool—
both man and woman— at one time or another.
Therefore, one should avoid that fire,
protecting even one's own life,
lest the forest-fire consume it.
The fire has a blackened path;
there, new shoots arise with the passing of days and nights.
But when a bhikkhu endowed with virtue burns with his fiery power,
neither his children nor his cattle [suffer].
Heirs obtain the wealth;
those who are without heirs and have no claimants become like the stumps of palm trees.
Therefore, indeed, a wise person,
seeing his own welfare,
[should avoid] both a serpent and fire.
One should conduct oneself properly toward a renowned kshatriya, and toward a bhikkhu endowed with virtue.
When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One:
"Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!
Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost..."
Or one might point out the way, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been declared by the Blessed One in many ways.
Therefore, venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.2 (SN 3.2, SN 113, PTS [1st ed. SN i 70, PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 162) 1. First Chapter*
The Discourse on Men.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, how many qualities, when arising within a person, arise for his harm, suffering, and discomfort?
“There are, great king, three qualities that, when arising within a person, arise for his harm, suffering, and discomfort.
Which three?
Greed, great king, is a state that, when arising within a person, arises for their harm, suffering, and discomfort.
Hatred, great king, is a state that, when arising within a person, arises for their harm, suffering, and discomfort.
Delusion, great king, is a state that, when arising within a person, arises for their harm, suffering, and discomfort.
“Great King, these three qualities, when arising within a person, arise for his harm, suffering, and lack of comfort.
Thus spoke [the Blessed One]...
“Greed, hatred, and delusion...”
A person of evil mind is destroyed by those things produced from within himself,
just as a tree of hollow bark is destroyed by its own fruit.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 3.3 (SN 3.3, SN 114, PTS [1st ed. SN i 71, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 163) 1.
First Chapter: The Discourse on Aging and Death (Jarāmaraṇa-sutta)
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, for one who is born, is there anything other than aging and death?”
“There is no escape from aging and death for one who is born, great king.

Even those wealthy, affluent, and opulent kṣatriya householders, possessing vast quantities of gold and silver, abundant assets and resources, and great wealth in money and grain—even for them, once born, there is no escape from aging and death.
And even those wealthy, affluent brahmins... [and so forth].”

There are great householders, wealthy, with vast riches and great enjoyments, possessing abundant gold and silver, abundant wealth and requisites, and abundant money and grain; even for them, there is no escaping birth, aging, and death.

And as for those monks, O Great King, who are arahants with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, whose fetters of existence are completely exhausted, and who are liberated through right knowledge—even their bodies are subject to dissolution.
“...it is subject to being laid down.
Thus spoke [the Blessed One]...
“Indeed, even the beautifully adorned royal chariots wear out;”
Moreover, even the body falls into decay;
but the Dhamma of the virtuous does not fall into decay,
for the good indeed proclaim it to the good.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.4 (SN 3.4, SN 115, PTS [1st ed. SN i 71, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 164) 1. First Chapter: The Chapter on the Pleasant (Paṭhamavagga) The Discourse on the Dear One (Piyasutta) “Monks, there are these four things that are dear, beloved, charming, and not disagreeable to oneself. What four? One’s mother, one’s father, one’s own dear son, and one’s own dear wife. These, monks, are the four things that are dear, beloved, charming, and not disagreeable to oneself. Just as, monks, these four things are dear, beloved, charming, and not disagreeable to oneself, so too, monks, there are these four things that are dear, beloved, charming, and not disagreeable to all beings and creatures. What four? Life, beauty, health, and happiness. These, monks, are the four things that are dear, beloved, charming, and not disagreeable to all beings and creatures. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will preserve our lives by means of what is dear, beloved, charming, and not disagreeable to ourselves. This is how you should train yourselves. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will preserve our beauty by means of what is dear, beloved, charming, and not disagreeable to ourselves. This is how you should train yourselves. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will preserve our health by means of what is dear, beloved, charming, and not disagreeable to ourselves. This is how you should train yourselves. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will preserve our happiness by means of what is dear, beloved, charming, and not disagreeable to ourselves. This is how you should train yourselves.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind:”
‘For whom, then, is the self dear, and for whom is the self not dear?
Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me:
‘Those who engage in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind—for them the self is not dear.’”
To them, the self is not dear.
Even though they might say,
"The self is dear to us," nevertheless, the self is not dear to them.
For what reason?
Whatever an unpleasant person might do to another unpleasant person, they do that very thing to themselves;
therefore, the self is unpleasant to them.
But those who practice good conduct with the body, good conduct with speech, and good conduct with the mind—
dear is the self to them.
Even though they might say this:
‘The self is not dear to us’; yet, on the contrary, the self is dear to them.
And why is that? For whatever one dear person would do for another dear person, that very thing they do to themselves by means of their own selves.
"Therefore, their own self is dear to them.
"So it is, Great King; so it is, Great King.
For whoever, Great King, engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, or misconduct by mind..."
Therefore, the self is not dear to them.
Even though they might say,
"The self is dear to us," nevertheless, the self is not dear to them.
For what reason?
Because, Great King, whatever one who is disliked might do to another who is disliked, that they do to themselves by themselves;
therefore, the self is disliked by them.
But as for those, Great King, who practice good conduct with the body, good conduct with speech, and good conduct with the mind—
for them, the self is dear.
Even though they might say this:
‘The self is not dear to us’;
yet, on the contrary, the self is dear to them. And why is that?
"For whatever one dear to oneself might do for another dear to oneself, great king, that they do to themselves by themselves;
therefore, the self is dear to them.
Thus he spoke... [and so forth].
“If one should know oneself as dear,
one should not yoke it to evil;
for that is not easily obtained.”
There is no happiness for one who has committed evil deeds when seized by the End-maker and abandoning human existence.
For what belongs to him?
And what does he take with him when he goes?
What is it that follows after him?
Like a shadow that never departs,
both merit and evil that a mortal performs here follow him.
For that indeed belongs to him;
taking that with him, he goes;
that alone is his follower.
Like a shadow that never departs.
Therefore, one should perform what is wholesome,
as a store for the life to come.
“Meritorious deeds are the foundation for living beings in the world beyond.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 3.5 (SN 3.5, SN 116, PTS [1st ed. SN i 72; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 166)
1. First Chapter:
Attarakkhita Sutta.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
As he was sitting to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, as I was here alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind:
‘Whose self, indeed, is guarded? Whose self is unguarded?’”
Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me:
"Those who engage in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind—
their self is unprotected."
Even though an elephant corps might protect them, or a cavalry corps might protect them, or a chariot corps might protect them, or an infantry corps might protect them;
nevertheless, their own selves remain unprotected. And why is that?
This is an external protection; it is not an internal protection.
Therefore, their self remains unprotected.
But those who practice good conduct with the body, practice good conduct with speech, and practice good conduct with the mind—
Their own selves are protected.
Even though neither an elephant corps would protect them, nor a cavalry corps, nor a chariot corps, nor an infantry corps would protect them;
nevertheless, their own selves are protected.
For what reason?
Because this protection is internal; it is not an external protection.
Therefore, their self is protected.”
“So it is, great king; so it is, great king.
For whoever, great king, engages in misconduct by way of the body … [as before] … their self is unprotected.”
For what reason?
Because, Great King, this protection is external; it is not an internal protection.
Therefore, their self remains unprotected.
For whoever, Great King, practices good conduct with the body, practices good conduct with speech, and practices good conduct with the mind—their self is protected.
Even though neither an elephant force would protect them, nor a cavalry force, nor a chariot force, nor an infantry force would protect them; [their self is still protected].
Then indeed their own self is protected.
For what reason?
Because this protection, Great King, is internal; it is not an external protection.
"Therefore, their self is protected.
This was said...
"Restraint in body is good;..."
Restraint in speech is good;
restraint in mind is good;
restraint in all things is good.
“Restraint in all things and a sense of shame—such a one is called ‘guarded.
— Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.6 (SN 3.6, SN 117, PTS [1st ed. SN i 73; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 168)
1. First Chapter: The Discourse on the Few.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
As King Pasenadi of Kosala was sitting to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind:

‘There are few beings in the world who, having obtained abundant and magnificent wealth, do not become intoxicated, do not become negligent, do not fall into greed for sensual pleasures, and do not act wrongly toward living beings.’”

“On the contrary, Mahārāja, it is far more numerous in this world those beings who, having obtained abundant and magnificent wealth, become intoxicated and negligent, fall into greed for sensual pleasures, and act wrongly toward other beings.
“It is so, Mahārāja; it is so, Mahārāja.

There are few, Mahārāja, those beings in this world who, having obtained abundant and magnificent wealth, do not become intoxicated, do not become negligent, do not fall into greed for sensual pleasures, and do not act wrongly toward other beings.”

"But rather, it is far more numerous those beings in the world who, having obtained abundant and magnificent wealth, become intoxicated and negligent, fall into greed for sensual pleasures, and act wrongly toward other beings.
Thus he spoke...
"They are infatuated with the enjoyment of sensual pleasures..."
Vultures, infatuated with sensual pleasures,
do not perceive their own ruin,
like deer caught in a laid trap.
"In the end it is bitter, for its ripening is evil.
— Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.7 (SN 3.7, SN 118, PTS 1st ed. SN i 74; PTS 2nd ed. SN i 170)
1. First Chapter:
The Discourse on the Gambling Hall.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, while sitting at the court of justice, I see wealthy great khattiyas, wealthy great brahmins,
and wealthy great householders— rich, of great wealth and vast possessions, with abundant gold and silver, and abundant means of enjoyment.”
“While possessing abundant wealth and grain, they speak deliberate lies for the sake of sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as their cause, and on account of sensual pleasures.
Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me:
‘Enough now with my business affairs; from now on, my good friend shall be known by his business affairs.’”
“So it is, great king; so it is, great king.

Those wealthy khattiya magnates, brahmin magnates, and householder magnates, O great king—rich, of great wealth and vast possessions, with abundant gold and silver, abundant means of subsistence, and abundant wealth and grain—who, for the sake of sensual pleasures and on account of sensual pleasures, [act thus]...”
“Out of desire, they speak a deliberate lie;
that will lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. This is what [the Blessed One] said... [and so forth].
“Infatuated with the enjoyment of sensual pleasures,
greedy for sense objects, and infatuated [with them],
they do not realize their own transgression.”
Like fish swiftly caught on a cast net,
it becomes bitter in its aftermath,
for its ripening is indeed evil.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.8 (SN 3.8, SN 119, PTS [1st ed. SN i 75, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 171) 1. First Chapter: The Discourse to Mallikā [The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then Queen Mallikā approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, how many things, when developed and cultivated, lead to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion? “There are, Mallikā, these three things which, when developed and cultivated, lead to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion. What three? Serenity, insight, and equanimity. These three things, Mallikā, when developed and cultivated, lead to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion. “But, venerable sir, how is serenity developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion? “Here, Mallikā, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called serenity. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called insight. Whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he dwells contemplating impermanence in it, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment. This is called equanimity. Thus, Mallikā, serenity is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion. “And how, venerable sir, is insight developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion? [The Blessed One replied: “Here, Mallikā, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called insight. Whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he dwells contemplating impermanence in it, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment. This is called equanimity. Thus, Mallikā, insight is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion. “And how, venerable sir, is equanimity developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion? [The Blessed One replied: “Here, Mallikā, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called equanimity. Whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he dwells contemplating impermanence in it, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment. This is called insight. Thus, Mallikā, equanimity is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, to the abandoning of hatred, to the abandoning of delusion. When this was said, Queen Mallikā said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to point out the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. “Mallikā, you are already a lay follower; why do you say this? “I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘In the past, there were disciples of the Blessed One who were arahants, whose taints were destroyed, who had lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and were completely liberated through final knowledge. It was because of hearing this that I went for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. “Mallikā, you are indeed a lay follower; why do you say this? “I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘In the past, there were disciples of the Blessed One who, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, were of spontaneous birth, due to attain Nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. It was because of hearing this that I went for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. “Mallikā, you are indeed a lay follower; why do you say this? “I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘In the past, there were disciples of the Blessed One who, with the destruction of three fetters and with the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, were once-returners, returning once more to this world to make an end of suffering.

It was because of hearing this that I went for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. “Mallikā, you are indeed a lay follower; why do you say this? “I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘In the past, there were disciples of the Blessed One who, with the destruction of three fetters, were stream-enterers, no longer subject to perdition, bound for enlightenment, assured, heading for Nibbāna. It was because of hearing this that I went for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. “Mallikā, you are indeed a lay follower; why do you say this? “I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘In the past, there were disciples of the Blessed One who, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, were of spontaneous birth, due to attain Nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. It was because of hearing this that I went for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. “Mallikā, you are indeed a lay follower; why do you say this? “I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘In the past, there were disciples of the Blessed One who, with the destruction of three fetters and with the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, were once-returners, returning once more to this world to make an end of suffering. It was because of hearing this that I went for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. “Mallikā, you are indeed a lay follower; why do you say this? “I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘In the past, there were disciples of the Blessed One who, with the destruction of three fetters, were stream-enterers, no longer subject to perdition, bound for enlightenment, assured, heading for Nibbāna. It was because of hearing this that I went for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. “Mallikā, you are indeed a lay follower; why do you say this? “I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘In the past, there were disciples of the Blessed One who, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, were of spontaneous birth, due to attain Nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. It was because of hearing this that I went for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. “Mallikā, you are indeed a lay follower; why do you say this? “I have heard this, venerable sir: ‘In the past, there were disciples of the Blessed One who, with the destruction of three fetters and with the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, were once-returners, returning once more to this world to make an end of suffering. It was because of hearing this that I went for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala had gone up to the excellent upper terrace of the palace together with Queen Mallikā.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to Queen Mallikā:
“Mallikā, is there anyone else dearer to you than yourself?
“There is no one else, Great King, dearer to me than myself.
But as for you, Great King, is there anyone else dearer to you than yourself?”
“Indeed, Mallikā, there is no one dearer to me than myself.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala descended from his palace and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala—
He said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, having gone to the upper terrace of the palace together with Queen Mallikā, I said to Queen Mallikā:
‘Mallikā, is there anyone else dearer to you than yourself?’”
When this was said, Bhante, Queen Mallikā said this to me:
“Great King, there is no one else dearer to me than myself.
But as for you, Great King, is there anyone else dearer to you than yourself?”
“Having been addressed thus, Bhante, I said to Queen Mallikā:
‘Mallikā, for me too there is no one dearer than myself.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion recited this verse:”
“Having wandered through all directions with my mind,
I found nothing anywhere dearer than myself.
Thus, each person holds their own self dear.”
"Therefore, one who desires their own welfare should not harm another.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 3.9 (SN 3.9, SN 120, PTS [1st ed. SN i 75, PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 172) 1. First Chapter.
The Sacrifice Discourse.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, a great sacrifice had been prepared for King Pasenadi of Kosala.
Five hundred bulls, five hundred young bulls, five hundred heifers, five hundred goats,
and five hundred rams were led to the sacrificial post for the sake of sacrifice.
And those who were his slaves, messengers, or laborers— they too, driven by the threat of punishment and driven by fear, performed the preliminary services with tearful faces, weeping.
Then, in the morning, a number of bhikkhus dressed themselves, took their bowls and robes, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after their meal and returning from their almsround, they approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side...
Those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, here a great sacrifice has been prepared for King Pasenadi of Kosala:
five hundred bulls, five hundred steers, five hundred heifers, and five hundred goats.”
"And five hundred bulls have been led to the sacrificial post for the sake of sacrifice.
And those who are his slaves, messengers, or laborers—even they, driven by sticks and driven by fear, with tearful faces and weeping, perform the preliminary services.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion recited these verses:
The horse sacrifice, the human sacrifice,
the *sammāpāsa*, the *vājapeyya*,
the *niraggaḷa*— these are great undertakings.
Those [offerings] do not yield great fruit where goats, sheep, cows,
and various other creatures are slaughtered.
The great seers who have gone rightly do not resort to that sacrifice which involves violence;
rather, they perform those sacrifices that are free from injury.
They always sacrifice in accordance with tradition;
neither goats nor sheep,
nor various cattle, are slain here.
The great seers who have gone rightly upon the path offer this sacrifice.
Let the wise person offer this sacrifice.
This sacrifice is of great fruit;
for one who performs it,
this is better and not worse.
"The sacrifice becomes vast, and the deities become pleased.
— *Saṁyutta Nikāya* 3.10 (SN 3.10, SN 121, PTS [1st ed. SN i 76, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 174)
Now at that time, a great multitude of people had been imprisoned by King Pasenadi of Kosala— some with ropes, some with fetters, and some with chains.
Then, in the morning, a number of bhikkhus dressed themselves, took their bowls and robes, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after their meal and returning from their almsround, they approached the Blessed One;

2. Second Chapter:
The Discourse on the Five Kings.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, while the five kings, headed by Pasenadi, were provided with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure and were enjoying themselves, this discussion arose among them:
"What, indeed, is the foremost of sensual pleasures?
Thereupon, some said this:
“Forms are the foremost of sensual pleasures,” some said; others said,
“Sounds are the foremost of sensual pleasures.”
Some said this:
"Fragrances are the foremost of sensual pleasures.
Others said this:
“Tastes are the foremost of sensual pleasures,” some say. Others say:
“Tangible objects are the foremost of sensual pleasures.”
When those kings were unable to persuade one another, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to them:
"Come, sirs, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached him, we shall question the Blessed One regarding this matter."
“We shall bear it in mind exactly as the Blessed One explains it.
“Very well, sirs,” those kings replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala.
Then those five kings, headed by Pasenadi, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, here, while we five kings—endowed with and possessed of the five cords of sensual pleasure—were enjoying ourselves, this discussion arose among us:”
“What, indeed, is the foremost of sensual pleasures?
Some said: “Forms are the foremost of sensual pleasures.”
Some said this:
“Sounds are the foremost of sensual pleasures.
Others said this:
‘Fragrances are the foremost of sensual pleasures. Some said:
‘Tastes are the foremost of sensual pleasures.’
Some said thus:
“Tangible objects are the foremost of sensual pleasures.
“But what, venerable sir, is the foremost of sensual pleasures?”
“Great King, I say that among the five cords of sensual pleasure, the pleasant is the foremost.
Great King, those very same forms are pleasing to one person, yet those same forms are unpleasing to another.
And whoever is satisfied with certain forms and has his purpose fulfilled by them does not yearn for any other form as superior or more excellent than those.”
Those forms are supreme for him;
those forms are unsurpassed for him.
Yet, Great King, those very same sounds are pleasing to some, while those very same sounds are displeasing to others.
And whoever is satisfied with these sounds and has fulfilled his intentions does not long for any other sound that is higher or more sublime than those.
Those sounds become supreme for him;
those sounds become unsurpassed for him.
Those very same fragrances, O Great King, are pleasing to some, while those same fragrances are unpleasing to others.
And whatever fragrance one is satisfied with and finds it fulfills one's intention, one does not long for another fragrance superior or more refined than that.
Those fragrances are supreme for that person.
Those fragrances are unsurpassed for him.
Likewise, Great King, those very tastes may be pleasing to one person, while those same tastes may be unpleasing to another.
And whoever is satisfied with certain tastes and has fulfilled their intention does not, because of those tastes, long for any other taste that is superior or more refined.
Those tastes are supreme for him;
those tastes are unsurpassed for him.
Yet, Great King, those same tangible objects are pleasing to one person, while those same tangible objects are unpleasing to another.
"And whoever is satisfied with these tangible objects and has fulfilled his intention does not long for another tangible object that is higher or more sublime than those.
Those tangible objects are supreme for him;
those tangible objects are unsurpassed for him."
Now at that time, the lay follower Candanaṅgalika was seated in that assembly.

“It occurs to me, Blessed One; it occurs to me, Sugata.”
“May it occur to you, Candanaṅgalika,” the Blessed One said.

behold the son of Aṅgīrasa shining forth,

2. Second Chapter:
The Discourse on the Doṇapāka Offering.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala was eating a meal of *doṇapāka* rice.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having finished his meal and being heavy-breathing, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that King Pasenadi of Kosala had finished his meal and was heavy-breathing, on that occasion recited this verse:
“For a person who is always mindful,
who knows the proper measure regarding the food he has obtained,
his painful feelings become slight.”
“Preserving his life, he ages slowly.
Now at that time, the young brahmin Sudassana was standing behind King Pasenadi of Kosala.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed the young brahmin Sudassana:
“Come, dear Sudassana, learn this verse from the Blessed One and recite it at every presentation of food for me.
And I shall provide you with a constant daily alms-offering of one hundred kahāpaṇas.

“For a person who is always mindful,
who knows the proper measure regarding food obtained,
his painful feelings become slight.”
“Preserving his life, he ages slowly.

“Both the welfare pertaining to the present life and that pertaining to the future life.
This is what [the Blessed One] said...
“Longevity, health, and beauty...”
Heaven, birth in a high-born family,
and successive, sublime delights— by one who yearns for these, [this path should be followed].
The wise praise heedfulness in the performance of meritorious deeds;
being heedful, one achieves both goals.
The wise person attains that which is beneficial both in this present life and that which is beneficial for the future life.
The steadfast one who has realized the goal is called wise.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 3.18 (SN 3.18, SN 129, PTS [1st ed. SN i 87; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 196)
2. Second Chapter:
The Discourse on Spiritual Friends (Kalyāṇamitta-sutta).
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind:

‘The Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One; and that is for one who has a good friend, a good companion, a good associate, and not for one who has a bad friend, a bad companion, a bad associate.’”
“So it is, Great King; so it is, Great King.
Well-expounded, Great King, is the Dhamma by me. But that is for one who has good friends, good companions, and good comrades, not for one who has evil friends, evil companions, and evil comrades.
Once, Great King, I was staying among the Sakyans at a town of the Sakyans named Nagaraka.”
Then, Great King, the bhikkhu Ānanda approached me; having approached, he paid homage to me and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Great King, the bhikkhu Ānanda said this to me:
“Venerable sir, this is half of the holy life: namely, good friendship, good companionship, and good comradeship.
When this was said, Great King, I said this to the bhikkhu Ānanda:
“Not so, Ānanda! Not so, Ānanda!
This entire holy life, Ānanda, is just this: having virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates.
For a monk who has virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates, it is to be expected that he will develop the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path.”
And how, Ānanda, does a bhikkhu who has good friends, good companions, and good associates develop the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path?

Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops right view, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment; he develops right intention... he develops right speech... he develops right action... [he develops right livelihood... he develops right effort... he develops right mindfulness... he develops right concentration, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment.
… he develops right livelihood … he develops right effort … he develops right mindfulness … he develops right concentration,
which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation,

and results in relinquishment. It is in this way, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu who has good friends, good companions, and good associates develops the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path.
"It should be understood, Ānanda, by this method how this entire holy life consists in this: namely, good friendship, good companionship, and good fellowship.
For it is by depending on me as a good friend, Ānanda, that beings subject to birth are freed from birth;
beings subject to aging are freed from aging; beings subject to illness are freed from illness; beings subject to death..."
“Beings are liberated from death; beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
It is by this method, Ānanda, that it should be understood how this entire holy life consists in this: namely, good friendship, good companionship, and good fellowship.
Therefore, Great King, you should train yourself thus:
‘I shall have virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates.
Thus, Great King, should you train yourself.
Relying upon this one quality, Great King, should you dwell—one who has virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates.
Heedfulness regarding wholesome states.
As you dwell heedfully, Great King, relying upon heedfulness while attending to the women’s quarters, this thought will arise:
“The king indeed dwells heedfully, relying upon heedfulness.”
"Come now, let us too dwell heedfully, relying upon heedfulness.
Great King, as you dwell heedfully, relying upon heedfulness, even the kshatriyas who follow you will think:
"The king indeed dwells heedfully, relying upon heedfulness."
"Come now, let us too dwell heedful, relying upon heedfulness.
As you dwell heedfully, Great King, relying upon heedfulness, your army will also think thus:
"The king indeed dwells heedfully, relying upon heedfulness."
‘Come now, let us too dwell diligently, relying upon diligence.
As you, Great King, dwell diligently, relying upon diligence, it will be said of the people of the towns and the countryside:
‘The king indeed dwells diligently, relying upon diligence.’”
“Come now, let us also dwell heedful, relying upon heedfulness.
“If you, Great King, dwell heedfully, relying upon heedfulness, then you yourself will be guarded and protected;
your harem will also be guarded and protected; and your treasury and granary will also be guarded and protected.”
Thus he spoke … [as before] … “By one who aspires to abundant and successive riches, [one should practice generosity].”
The wise praise heedfulness in the performance of meritorious deeds;
being heedful, one achieves both goals.
The wise person attains it:
whatever benefit there is in this present life,
and whatever benefit there is in the future life.
The steadfast one who has realized the goal is called wise.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 3.19 (SN 3.19, SN 130, PTS [1st ed. SN i 89; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 201)
2. Second Chapter.
First Discourse on Childlessness.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One during the middle of the day;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As King Pasenadi of Kosala was sitting there to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Why then, Great King, have you come here from the midst of the day?
“Venerable sir, here in Sāvatthī a householder who was a wealthy merchant has passed away.
Having brought his estate—which he left behind because he had no son—into the royal palace, I am now returning.”
"Eighty hundred thousand [pieces] of gold, venerable sir, let alone silver.
Moreover, venerable sir, such was the food-provision of that householder merchant:
he ate broken rice with sour gruel as his second course."
Such was his clothing:
he wore a lower garment made of triple-layered hemp.
Such was his vehicle:
“He travels in a rickety little chariot with a leaf-umbrella being held over him.
“It is so, Great King, it is so, Great King.
A person of no integrity, Great King, having obtained abundant wealth, neither makes himself happy and joyful, nor his mother and father...”
He does not provide comfort and nourishment for himself, nor does he provide comfort and nourishment for his wife and children, nor for his slaves, laborers, and servants,
nor for his friends and colleagues; he does not establish a lofty sacrificial gift among ascetics and brahmins that leads to heaven,
has a happy result, and conduces to rebirth in the celestial realms.
When those possessions of yours are not thus rightly enjoyed, kings take them away, or thieves take them away, or fire burns them, or water carries them away, or unloved heirs take them away.
In this way, Great King, those possessions of yours, being not rightly enjoyed, go to ruin rather than to enjoyment.
It is just as if, Great King, there were a lotus pond in a place frequented by non-humans, with clear water, cool water, sweet water, pure water, with good landing places, and delightful.
People would neither take it away, nor drink it, nor bathe in it, nor use it for any purpose whatsoever.
For in this way, Great King, that water, being properly unused, would go to exhaustion rather than to enjoyment.
Even so, Great King, an untrue person, having obtained magnificent wealth, neither makes himself happy nor gladdens himself.

He does not bring happiness or satisfaction to his mother and father; he does not bring happiness or satisfaction to his wife and children; he does not bring happiness or satisfaction to his slaves, laborers, and servants;

he does not bring happiness or satisfaction to his friends and colleagues; nor does he establish an uplifting offering among ascetics and brahmins that leads to heaven, has a happy result, and conduces to rebirth in the celestial realms.
When those possessions of yours are not thus rightly enjoyed, kings take them away, or thieves take them away, or fire burns them, or water carries them away, or unloved heirs take them away.
In this way, Great King, those possessions of yours, when not rightly enjoyed, go to ruin rather than to enjoyment.
But a person of integrity, Great King, having obtained abundant wealth, makes himself happy and satisfied, [and likewise his] mother and father.
He comforts and delights himself; he comforts and delights his wife and children; he comforts and delights his slaves, laborers, and servants; he comforts and delights his friends and colleagues;
and he establishes among ascetics and brahmins a lofty sacrificial gift that leads to heaven, has a happy result, and conduces to rebirth in the celestial realms.
While he thus rightly enjoys those wealth resources, neither kings take them away, nor thieves steal them, nor fire burns them, nor water sweeps them away, nor unwelcome heirs take them.
In this way, Great King, when your wealth is used rightly, it comes to enjoyment rather than exhaustion.
It is just as if, Great King, there were a lotus pond not far from a village or a town, with clear water, cool water, sweet water, pure water, with beautiful landing places, and delightful.
People might take that water away, drink it, bathe in it, or use it for their various needs.
For in this way, Great King, that water, being used properly, would go toward enjoyment rather than exhaustion.
Even so, Great King, a virtuous person, having obtained abundant wealth, makes himself happy and satisfied; he makes his mother and father happy and satisfied;
he makes his wife and children happy and satisfied; he makes his slaves, laborers, and servants happy and satisfied; and he makes his friends and colleagues happy and satisfied.
He comforts and delights them; he establishes among recluses and brahmins a high-priestly offering that leads to heaven, has a happy result, and conduces to rebirth in the celestial realms.
When his wealth is thus rightly enjoyed, kings do not seize it, thieves do not steal it, fire does not burn it, water does not sweep it away, and unpleasant heirs do not take it.
In this way, Great King, when your wealth is rightly enjoyed, it serves as enjoyment rather than going to ruin.”
“Just as cool water in a desolate place dries up when it is not drunk,
so too does a base person, having acquired wealth, [squander it].”
He does not enjoy [wealth] for himself nor does he give it away.
But the wise and discerning person, having acquired wealth,
enjoys it and performs his duties.
Thus, having supported his circle of kinsmen, the bull goes blamelessly to the heavenly realm.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 3.20 (SN 3.20, SN 131, PTS [1st ed. SN i 91, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 205)
2. The Second Chapter:

The Second Discourse on Sonlessness Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One during the middle of the day. Having approached and sat down to one side, the Blessed One said this to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
“Now then, Great King, from where have you come so early in the day?
“Venerable sir, here in Sāvatthī a householder who was a treasurer has passed away.
Having brought his estate—which he left behind with no son—into the royal palace, I am now returning.”
"Lord, there were hundreds of thousands of pieces of gold, not to mention silver.
Yet, Lord, such was the food-provision of that householder merchant:
he ate broken rice with sour gruel as his second course."
Such was his clothing:
he wore a lower garment made of three layers of hemp.
Such was his vehicle:
“He travels in a dilapidated little chariot with a leaf-parasol being held over him.
“It is so, Great King; it is so, Great King.
Once upon a time, Great King, that householder merchant provided almsfood to the Paccekasambuddha named Tagarasikhī.”
Having said, “Give almsfood to the ascetic,” he rose from his seat and departed.
But after giving it, he later felt regret, thinking:
“It would have been better if these slaves or laborers had eaten this almsfood.”
Moreover, he deprived his only son of life for the sake of his wealth.

However, Mahārāja, because that householder merchant provided almsfood to the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī, as the ripening of that karma, he was reborn seven times in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.
And by the remaining ripening of that very same karma, he served as the guild-leader in this very Sāvatthī seven times.
Because that householder treasurer, O Great King, felt regret after giving and thought,
"It would have been better if these alms-foods had been eaten by slaves or laborers," as the ripening of that karma,
his mind does not incline toward enjoying abundant food, nor does his mind incline toward enjoying abundant clothing.
His mind does not incline toward the enjoyment of grand vehicles, nor does his mind incline toward the enjoyment of the fivefold luxury of the great sensual pleasures.
However, Great King, because that householder merchant deprived his brother’s only son of life for the sake of his inheritance,
as the ripening of that kamma, for many years, for many hundreds of years...
He was roasted in hell for many thousands of years and hundreds of thousands of years.
By the remaining ripening of that very same karma, he now causes this seventh estate without an heir to enter the royal treasury.
Great King, for that merchant householder, former merit has been exhausted and no new merit has been accumulated.
“But today, Great King, that householder merchant is being cooked in the Mahāroruva hell.
“Is it so, venerable sir? Has the householder merchant been reborn in the Mahāroruva hell?
“It is so, Great King; the householder merchant has been reborn in the Mahāroruva hell.”
This is what he said...
[and so forth]... "Grain, wealth, silver, gold, or whatever property one may possess;”
Servants, laborers, messengers,
and those who depend on him for their livelihood—
all must go taking nothing at all.
Everything that goes to be laid down—
whatever one does by way of body,
speech, or mind.
For that indeed belongs to him;
taking that with him, he goes;
that alone is his follower.
Like a shadow that never departs.
Therefore, one should perform what is wholesome,
as a store for the world beyond.
“Meritorious deeds are the foundation for living beings in the world beyond.
The second chapter.
Its summary verse:
The matted-hair ascetics, the five kings,
and the rice-porridge and sprout.
Two were spoken by Saṅgāma,
two by Mallikā and by Appamāda;
two were spoken by Aputtaka.
Therefore it is called a chapter.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 3.21 (SN 3.21, SN 132, PTS [1st ed] SN i 93, PTS [2nd ed] SN i 209) 3.
Third Chapter.
The Discourse on Persons.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached, he [greeted] the Blessed One...
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. As King Pasenadi of Kosala was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Great King, these four types of persons are found existing in the world.
Which four?"
One who goes from darkness to darkness,
one who goes from darkness to light,
and one who goes from light to darkness.
One whose ultimate destination is light.
And how, Great King, is a person one whose ultimate destination is darkness?
Here, Great King, a certain person is reborn into a low family—either a family of outcasts (caṇḍāla) or a family of bamboo-workers (venaka).
Or he may be born into a family of hunters, or a family of chariot-makers, or a family of scavengers— poor, with little food and drink, living in hardship,
where even basic sustenance and clothing are obtained only with great difficulty.
Furthermore, he is ugly, unsightly, deformed, afflicted by many diseases, or one-eyed, or a cripple, or lame, or paralyzed on one side.
Or, not obtaining food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes,
ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lighting, he engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind. Having engaged in misconduct by body,
misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
"Just as if, great king, a man were to go from darkness to darkness, or from gloom to gloom, or from a stain of blood to a stain of blood—
such, great king, do I say this person is.
In this way, great king, a person is one who goes from darkness to darkness."
And how, Great King, is a person one who goes from darkness to light?
Here, Great King, a certain person is reborn into a low family— such as a family of candālas, or a family of weavers, or a family of hunters,
or a family of chariot-makers, or a family of scavengers— a family that is poor, lacking in food and drink, and living in hardship.
Where food and clothing are obtained only with great difficulty;
and where one is moreover ugly, unsightly, deformed, and afflicted by many diseases— whether blind, or with crooked limbs, or lame, or paralyzed in an arm—
such a person does not obtain food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lighting.
Thus he practices good conduct with the body, he practices good conduct with speech, and he practices good conduct with the mind.

Having practiced good conduct with the body, having practiced good conduct with speech, and having practiced good conduct with the mind, at the breaking up of the body, after death, he reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.

Great King, it is just as if a man were to mount a couch from the ground, or mount the back of a horse from a couch, or mount the neck of an elephant from the back of a horse, or mount a palace from the neck of an elephant.
"O Great King, I describe this person as being just like that.
Thus, O Great King, is a person one who goes from darkness to light.
And how, O Great King, is a person one who goes from light to light?"
In this case, Great King, a certain person is reborn into a high family— either a prominent khattiya family, a prominent brahmin family,
or a prominent householder family— one that is wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, with abundant gold and silver, abundant assets and requisites,
and abundant wealth and grain.

And he is handsome, pleasing to behold, and inspiring; he is endowed with the highest excellence of complexion and is a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lighting.
Yet he engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Thus, having practiced misconduct by body, having practiced misconduct by speech, and having practiced misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell. It is just as if, Great King,
a man were to descend from a palace onto the back of an elephant, or from the back of an elephant onto the back of a horse,
or from the back of a horse onto a couch, or from a couch onto the ground.
Or as if one were to enter the darkness of the earth.
It is just like this, Great King, that I describe such a person.
In this way, Great King, a person has light as their ultimate destination.
And how, Great King, is a person one whose destiny is from light to light?
Here, Great King, a certain person is reborn into a high family—
either a wealthy khattiya family, a wealthy brahmin family, or a wealthy householder family— one that is affluent, possessing great wealth and vast enjoyments, with abundant gold and silver.
He possesses abundant wealth and resources, abundant money and grain.

He is handsome, pleasing to behold, and inspiring; he is endowed with the highest excellence of complexion. He is a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
He practices good conduct by way of body, he practices good conduct by way of speech, and he practices good conduct by way of mind.

Thus, having practiced good conduct with the body, having practiced good conduct with speech, and having practiced good conduct with the mind, at the breaking up of the body, after death, he reappears in a happy destination, a heavenly world.

Great King, it is just as if a man were to move from one couch to another couch, or from the back of a horse to the back of another horse, or from the shoulder of one elephant to the shoulder of another elephant, or from one palace to another palace.
It is in this very way, Great King, that I describe this person.
"In this way, great king, a person is one whose destination is light after light.
These, great king, are the four types of persons existing and found in the world.
Thus spoke [the Blessed One]... [and so forth].
“A poor man, O King,
is faithless and stingy;
he is miserly and of evil intent.”
Wrong view and lack of respect toward ascetics or brahmins,
or even toward other mendicants.
He reviles and insults;
he is a nihilist and a provoker.
He forbids one who is giving.
To those begging for food—
such a person as this, O King,
lord of men, when he is dying;
A man who is destitute, O King, goes to a terrible hell, destined for darkness after darkness.
He is faithful and free from stinginess;
the person who gives with the highest intention and an undistracted mind.
Whether it be ascetics or brahmins,
or others who are mendicants,
one rises and pays homage to them.
He trains in even conduct:
he does not prevent one who is giving food to those who ask.
Such a person, O King,
lord of men, when dying,
goes to the realm of the Thirty-three.
One who goes from darkness to light.
O King, even if a man is wealthy,
if he is faithless and stingy;
Avaricious, evil-intentioned,
holding wrong views, and disrespectful toward ascetics or brahmins—
Or even other mendicants;
he reviles and insults them,
being a nihilist and a harasser.
O King, such a person who prevents food from being given to those who beg for it—
Being measured out, O lord of people,
he goes to a terrible hell,
with his life-breath as his only refuge.
If a man is wealthy, O King,
and is faithful and free from stinginess,
he gives with a noble intention.
A person with an undistracted mind [should give] to ascetics or brahmins,
or even to other mendicants.
Rising, he pays homage;
he trains in even conduct.
He does not forbid one who is giving.
To those begging for food—
such a man as this, O King,
lord of people, when he is dying;
“He goes to the realm of the Thirty-three, destined for light after light.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 3.22 (SN 3.22, SN 133, PTS [1st ed. SN i 96, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 216)
3. Third Chapter:
The Discourse on Grandmothers. At Sāvatthī.
As King Pasenadi of Kosala was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Well now, Great King, where have you come from in the middle of the day?
“Venerable sir, my grandmother has passed away; she was aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life, having reached a hundred and twenty years of age.”
"Venerable sir, my grandmother was dear and pleasing to me.
If, venerable sir, I could obtain the elephant-treasure on the condition that 'may my grandmother not pass away,' I would give even the elephant-treasure, thinking:
'May my grandmother not pass away.'"
“Venerable sir, if I could obtain a horse-treasure on the condition that my grandmother did not pass away, I would give away the horse-treasure so that my grandmother might not pass away.
If I could obtain a choice village on the condition that my grandmother did not pass away, I would give away the choice village so that my grandmother might not pass away.”
‘May my grandmother not have passed away.
Venerable sir, if I could obtain even a portion of a district on the condition that ‘may my grandmother not have passed away,’ I would give even that portion of a district:
‘may my grandmother not have passed away.’”
“‘All beings, great king, are subject to death; death is their end; they have not transcended death.
‘It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir!
How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: “All beings, great king, are subject to death; death is their end; they have not transcended death.”’”
"All beings are subject to death, have death as their end, and have not transcended death.
"So it is, Great King; so it is, Great King.
All beings are subject to death, have death as their end, and have not transcended death."
“Just as, great king, whatever clay vessels there may be—whether unbaked or baked—all of them are subject to breaking, end in breaking, and do not transcend breaking;
even so, great king, all beings are subject to death, end in death, and do not transcend death.
This is what [the Blessed One] said... [etc.]
“All beings will die,
for life ends in death;
they will go according to their karma.”
They experience the fruits of merit and evil:
those of evil deeds go to hell,
while those of meritorious deeds go to a happy destination.
Therefore, one should perform what is wholesome,
an accumulation for the future life;
for merits follow one into the world beyond.
“They are the support for living beings.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 3.23 (SN 3.23, SN 134, PTS (1st ed. SN i 98, PTS (2nd ed. SN i 218) 3.
Third Chapter (Tatiyavagga)
The Discourse on the World. At Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, how many things arise in the world that lead to harm, suffering, and an unhappy dwelling?
“There are, great king, three things that arise in the world that lead to harm, suffering, and an unhappy dwelling.
Which three?”
Greed, O Great King, is a phenomenon of the world; when it arises, it arises for one's detriment, for suffering, and for an unhappy dwelling.
Hatred, O Great King, is a phenomenon of the world; when it arises, it arises for one's detriment, for suffering, and for an unhappy dwelling.
Delusion, O Great King, is a phenomenon of the world; when it arises, it arises for one's detriment, for suffering, and for an unhappy dwelling.
“Great King, these three things, when they arise in the world, arise for one’s harm, for one’s suffering, and for one’s lack of well-being.
Thus spoke [the Blessed One]...
“Greed, hatred, and delusion...”
A person of evil mind is destroyed by those things produced from within himself,
just as a bamboo is destroyed by its own fruit.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 3.24 (SN 3.24, SN 135, PTS [1st ed. SN i 98, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 219) 3. Tatiyavagga Issattasutta The Discourse on Archery "Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to shoot an arrow from a bow. It would not fall down midway until it had reached its goal. Why is that? Because it has gained a support. So too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of faith, he does not fall down midway until he has reached his goal. Why is that? Because he has gained a support. "And what, bhikkhus, is the support for a bhikkhu? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the support for a bhikkhu."
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, where indeed should a gift be given?”
“Wherever, Great King, the mind finds confidence.
“But where, venerable sir, is a gift given that bears great fruit?
“This, Great King, is one matter—where a gift should be given—and this is another—where a gift, once given, bears great fruit.”
"Great King, what is given to one who is virtuous bears great fruit, but not so to one who is immoral.
Therefore, Great King, I shall question you about this very matter. Answer as you see fit.
What do you think, Great King?"
"Suppose a battle were set before him and the conflict had drawn up its ranks.
Then a young nobleman might arrive who was untrained, unskilled, unpracticed, and inexperienced—one who is timid, nervous, terrified, and prone to flight.
Would you support such a man, or would you have need for a man such as that?"
“I would not support that man, venerable sir, nor do I have any need for such a man.
“Then suppose a brahmin youth were to come who was untrained...
[and so on] ...then suppose a vessa youth were to come who was untrained... [and so on].
“Now suppose a young Śūdra were to arrive, untrained...
[and so on] ...I have no need for such a man.
“What do you think of that, Great King?”
"Suppose here a battle were set before him and a conflict arrayed for combat.
Then a noble youth might come—well-trained, skilled in hand, experienced, having undergone practice, fearless, undaunted, unafraid, and not fleeing.
Would you support that man, and would you have need of such a man?"
“I would hire that man, Bhante, for I have need of such a man.
“Then suppose a young brahmin were to come along...
[as before] ...then suppose a young vessa were to come along... [as before]...”
“Now suppose a young Sudda were to come, well-trained, skilled in hand, disciplined, experienced, fearless, undaunted, unafraid, and not fleeing.
Would you support such a man, and would you have need for such a man?
“I would support him, venerable sir, and I would have need for such a man.”

“In the same way, Great King, whoever has gone forth from the home life into homelessness from whatever family, if he has abandoned five factors and is endowed with five factors, what is given to him yields great fruit.
Which five factors have been abandoned?

Sensual desire has been abandoned; ill will has been abandoned; sloth and torpor have been abandoned; restlessness and remorse have been abandoned; doubt has been abandoned. Which five factors is he endowed with?”
These five factors have been abandoned.
With which five factors is he endowed?
He is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training; he is endowed with the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training.
He possesses the aggregate of morality of one beyond training, he possesses the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, he possesses the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training,
he possesses the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training, and he possesses the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.
Thus, he is endowed with these five factors.
"Thus, what is given to one who has abandoned five factors and is endowed with five factors yields great fruit.
This is what the Blessed One said... [as before] ...the Teacher.
“The king, seeking victory in battle,
should support that youth in whom skill, strength, and energy are found.”
Not harshness, due to birth as a condition.
Likewise, patience and gentleness—
those qualities upon which he is firmly established;
One should honor the wise person of noble conduct,
even if they are of low birth;
one should cause delightful hermitages to be built.
One should dwell here with those who are learned;
one should create clearings in the jungle and causeways across difficult terrain.
One should give food, drink, hard food, and also clothing and lodgings to those who have become upright.
With a mind that is perfectly serene.
Just as a cloud, thundering and garlanded with lightning,
possesses a hundred peaks;
It fills the heights and the depths,
raining down upon the earth;
even so does the one endowed with faith and learned in the Dhamma.
Having prepared food,
the wise man satisfies the mendicants with food and drink.
Rejoicing, he scatters [the gifts] and cries out, "Give! Give!"—
for that indeed is his thundering.
Just as from a god raining down;
that vast stream of merit rains down upon the giver.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.25 (SN 3.25, SN 136, PTS [1st ed. SN i 100, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 224) 3. The Third Chapter: The Simile of the Mountain The Discourse on the Simile of the Mountain At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, suppose a mountain peak were to rise up into the sky, solid, one mass, reaching to the heavens. A man would come along, desiring to see the world, wishing to see the world. He would stand on the eastern side of that mountain peak and think: ‘I do not see the world, nor do I see what pertains to the world. Then he would walk around that mountain peak to the southern side, and there too he would think: ‘I do not see the world, nor do I see what pertains to the world. Then he would walk around it to the western side, and there too he would think: ‘I do not see the world, nor do I see what pertains to the world. Then he would walk around it to the northern side, and there too he would think: ‘I do not see the world, nor do I see what pertains to the world. “Bhikkhus, this simile was given by the Blessed One with reference to the five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates subject to clinging. “Just as that mountain peak rising up into the sky, solid, one mass, reaching to the heavens, so too, bhikkhus, these five aggregates subject to clinging are like a mountain peak. When a noble disciple has seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, he does not regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He does not regard feeling as self... perception as self... volitional formations as self... consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. “When he does not regard them in such ways, he is not attached to anything in the world. Being unattached, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains nibbāna. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
As King Pasenadi of Kosala was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Well now, Great King, from where have you come so soon after midday?”
“Venerable sir, those royal duties that belong to anointed khattiya kings— who are intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty, overwhelmed by the lure of sensual pleasures,
who have attained stability over their territories and dwell having conquered a great circle of the earth—
I am now intent upon those.”
“What do you think, great king?
Suppose a man were to come to you from the eastern direction, trustworthy and reliable.
He would approach you and say:”
“Come now, Great King, you should know this: I am coming from the eastern direction.
There I saw a great mountain, level with the clouds, approaching while crushing all living beings.
Do whatever must be done, Great King.”
Then a second person might come from the western direction...
then a third person might come from the northern direction...
then a fourth person might come from the southern direction—one who is trustworthy and reliable.
Then, having approached him, one should say:
"Truly, Great King, you should know this: I am coming from the southern direction.
There I saw a great mountain, level with the clouds, coming along crushing all living beings."
“Whatever must be done, O Great King, do that.
“In such a situation, O Great King, when this great and terrible danger has arisen—a dreadful destruction of humanity, where human birth is so difficult to obtain—what should be done?
“In such a situation, venerable sir, when this great and terrible danger has arisen—a dreadful destruction of humanity, where human birth is so difficult to obtain—”

“What else is there for him to do, other than practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, other than practicing in equanimity, other than performing wholesome deeds, other than performing meritorious deeds?
“I announce this to you, Great King; I declare this to you, Great King: aging and death are indeed overtaking you.”
“If aging and death are advancing upon you, Great King, what should be done?

“Venerable sir, when aging and death are advancing upon me, what else should be done but the practice of the Dhamma, the practice of righteousness, the performance of wholesome deeds, and the performance of meritorious deeds?
For those, venerable sir, who are anointed Kṣatriya kings, intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty and overwhelmed by the lure of sensual pleasures...”
For those who have attained stability over their territories and dwell having conquered a great circle of the earth, there are elephant battles;
yet even for them, venerable sir, there is no escape, there is no domain, as old age and death roll on.
And as for those kings, the kṣatriyas, who have been anointed on the head... [and so forth].
For those who dwell there, horse battles occur...
chariot battles occur... infantry battles occur; ...pe...;
[and so on]... infantry battles occur.
"Venerable sir, even for those battles with weapons there is no recourse, no domain, when aging and death are rolling in.
Furthermore, venerable sir, in this royal court there are wise ministers who are capable of sowing dissension among incoming enemies through counsel.
Yet, venerable sir, even for those battles of counsel there is no recourse, no domain, when aging and death are rolling in."

"Moreover, venerable sir, there exists in this royal family abundant bullion and gold, both stored underground and kept above ground, with which we are able to appease any enemies who have arrived by means of wealth.
Yet, venerable sir, for those battles fought over wealth, there is no escape, there is no domain [of safety] while aging and death are rolling on.

And while aging and death are rolling on, venerable sir, what else should be done but the practice of the Dhamma, the practice of righteousness, the performance of wholesome deeds, and the performance of meritorious deeds?"
“So it is, Great King, so it is, Great King.

When aging and death are rolling in, what else is there to be done but the practice of the Dhamma, the practice of righteousness, the performance of wholesome deeds, and the performance of meritorious deeds?
Thus spoke the Blessed One… [as before]…
The Teacher said:
"Just as vast mountains of rock,
reaching up to touch the sky;"
They would march all around,
crushing [everything] in the four directions;
even so are old age and death.
They approach the Pāṇinīs:
the khattiyas, the brahmins, the vessas,
the suddas, and the caṇḍālas and pukkusas.
It avoids nothing;
it crushes everything.
There is no ground there for elephants.
Not by chariots, nor by infantry,
nor even by battle of spells,
nor by wealth, is it possible to conquer them.
Therefore, indeed, a wise person,
seeing his own welfare,
[should place confidence] in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
The wise person should establish faith.
Whoever practices the Dhamma by means of body,
speech, and mind;
“Right here they praise him,
and after passing away, he rejoices in heaven.
Thus ends the third chapter.
Its summary verse:
Person, grandmother, the world,
lordship, and the mountain simile.
This "Fivefold Discourse on Kosala," taught by the Best of Buddhas, is concluded.
The Saṃyutta Nikāya on Kosala is complete.
